tldr: We propose P³-WAM, a unified world action model for egocentric dexterous manipulation. It jointly trains 3D hand motion reconstruction from video (Perceive), future video prediction conditioned on specified actions (Predict), and concurrent action-and-video planning from instructions or goal images (Plan) using a single diffusion transformer. Training these three tasks together boosts their mutual performance, outperforming specialized models in 3D reconstruction accuracy and video prediction quality while also demonstrating successful action transfer to real robot hardware.
hero_caption: An overview of P³-WAM. It consistently handles three complementary modes within a single model: Perceive, which reconstructs 3D hand and camera trajectories from video; Predict, which generates future video from specified hand and camera actions; and Plan, which jointly generates action trajectories and visual futures from language instructions and goal images.
overview:
To achieve dexterous manipulation in robots, simply looking at camera images and moving a robot arm is not enough. Like a human child, three capabilities must be tightly coupled: understanding "what just happened" (Perceive), imagining "how the world changes if I move like this" (Predict), and determining "how I should move to achieve a goal" (Plan).

However, prior research has developed these as separate, isolated methods: 3D hand shape and camera trajectory reconstruction from monocular video, action-conditioned video generation (world models), and joint action-and-video generation (world action models). Solving them separately prevents an essential understanding that connects actions to their physical outcomes.

To address this, the authors developed P³-WAM, which jointly learns these three modes (Perceive, Predict, and Plan) within a single diffusion transformer (DiT). Built upon a strong pretrained video foundation model (Wan2.2), it introduces compact 3D hand joint and camera pose tokens in MANO format and achieves bidirectional visual–action attention through a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture. During training, by randomly toggling which parts of video and actions are shown or hidden, the exact same model is trained to solve all three tasks.

Experimental results show that the unified model trained on all tasks outperforms models trained on each task individually across all fronts. Compared to specialized baselines, it significantly cuts 3D hand reconstruction (Perceive) errors, improves video prediction (Predict) quality, and substantially enhances adherence to language instructions and goal images in planning (Plan). The authors also demonstrate that the generated human hand trajectories can be retargeted and executed on a real robot hand.
contributions: Proposed P³-WAM, a world action model for egocentric dexterous manipulation that solves 3D interaction reconstruction (Perceive), action-conditioned world prediction (Predict), and goal-directed planning (Plan) within a single unified framework

Introduced a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture with shared base weights from a pretrained video diffusion model, combined with action-dedicated experts equipped with LoRA and bidirectional attention to tightly couple video and 3D actions

Showed that a training strategy with randomized masking of video and action visibility allows perception, prediction, and planning to mutually reinforce each other, outperforming specialized baselines in each task
Demonstrated that the generated 3D human hand trajectories can be retargeted into joint commands for a dexterous robot hand, enabling real-world execution on physical hardware

sections.heading: Why tie seeing, predicting, and planning into one?
sections.summary: For robots to manipulate dexterously, the abilities to perceive observed actions in 3D, predict world changes from actions, and plan goal-directed actions are essential. Unifying these three previously separated capabilities into a single world action model, P³-WAM, unlocks their mutual synergies.
sections.details:
In building robots that perform dexterous manipulation, simply converting input images into actions has its limits. A truly intelligent embodied model must be able to answer three fundamental questions:
- What just happened? (Perceive: the ability to recognize 3D hand motion and camera movement from video)
- How will the world change if I move like this? (Predict: the ability to forecast physical world dynamics given specified actions)
- What should I do to achieve the goal? (Plan: the ability to assemble action trajectories and anticipated visual consequences toward a target state)

Human children learn by observing adults' movements and acquire causal relationships between actions and outcomes through trial and error. In other words, a common core of physical knowledge—"actions and their consequences"—must underlie all three abilities.

However, prior research has progressed under separate frameworks: 3D hand pose reconstruction from monocular video, action-conditioned video prediction world models, and goal-directed world action models. The starting point of this paper is to unite them within a single model rather than treating them separately.

The proposed P³-WAM is built on a pretrained video diffusion transformer (Wan2.2). It integrates bimanual 3D joint poses and camera motion as compact tokens, adopting a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture that handles video and actions together. By stochastically varying the given conditioning context and hidden prediction targets during training, a single model learns all three modes simultaneously. As a result, unified training across tasks elevates performance across all capabilities compared to training tasks in isolation, revealing a remarkable mechanism of mutual reinforcement.

sections.heading: Trends in world models, 3D hand reconstruction, and multimodal unification
sections.summary: This work sits at the intersection of three fields: video world models, monocular 3D hand reconstruction, and multimodal unified models. It bridges the gap between video and action, as well as the fragmentation between tasks found in prior approaches.
sections.details:
Related work can be organized into three main lines:

### Video World Models and World Action Models
As world models for robot action, methods that generate future images or videos conditioned on actions (such as Cosmos and Wan) are advancing rapidly. However, when dealing with dexterous manipulation, latent actions alone lack spatial precision, leaving the challenge of how to incorporate explicit geometric structures like meshes or 3D keypoints. Furthermore, while World Action Models (WAMs) that jointly generate future video and action trajectories have emerged recently, video and action generation remain loosely coupled, and 3D geometric perception is often missing.

### Monocular 3D Hand Reconstruction
Techniques that reconstruct 3D hand pose and shape from a single camera (such as HaMeR and WiLoR) have seen major accuracy gains on single images thanks to scaling Transformers. However, in egocentric scenes where the camera moves and interacts with objects across an entire video, occlusions (hands and objects blocking each other) and left-right confusion still occur frequently. Recently, attempts to leverage the strong prior knowledge of video diffusion models (such as ViDiHand) have begun, but no prior work trains hand reconstruction jointly with future prediction and planning capabilities like this paper does.

### Multimodal Unified Models
Research that solves diverse tasks within a single model by switching input and output modalities (such as Unified World Models) has also been increasing. P³-WAM extends this idea uniquely to articulated hand motion, a domain demanding extreme degrees of freedom and precision. Rather than simply generating images, it integrates explicit 3D hand parameters and camera trajectories deep inside the video diffusion model.

sections.heading: How P³-WAM works: Co-locating 3D actions within a video diffusion model
sections.summary: P³-WAM features an architecture that shares the backbone weights of a pretrained video generation model while incorporating action-dedicated experts for 3D hand and camera poses. By randomly controlling input masking, a single model flexibly toggles between the Perceive, Predict, and Plan modes.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Unified Task Formulation
The model operates on egocentric video $\mathbf{V}$ and time-synchronized 3D action sequences $\mathbf{A}$. Here, action $\mathbf{a}_t$ is defined as a pair consisting of bimanual MANO parameters (joint rotations, shape, etc.) $\mathbf{h}_t$ and the relative camera pose $\mathbf{P}_t$ from the initial frame.
- Perceive mode: Given the full video, it reconstructs the 3D action sequence.
- Predict mode: Given the initial image, instruction text, and the 3D action sequence to execute, it generates the future video.
- Plan mode: Given the initial image and instruction text (and optionally a goal image), it jointly generates the 3D action sequence and future video.

### 3.2 Joint Modeling of Video and Actions
P³-WAM builds upon the pretrained Wan2.2 video diffusion transformer (DiT). To tightly couple video and actions, it combines two approaches (Figure F3):
1. Spatial control signals: 2D skeleton videos rendered from 3D hand poses are converted into latents via a video VAE and concatenated with RGB inputs. Camera poses are converted into Plücker coordinate ray maps and added to the DiT patch embeddings.
2. Bidirectional attention: A pretrained, frozen Action Autoencoder compresses each frame's hands (left and right) and camera into compact 64-dimensional tokens each. Inside the DiT, the RGB expert and Action expert share base projection weights, while the Action expert is adapted with LoRA (rank 128). Their tokens are concatenated and attend to each other bidirectionally, fully blending the visual context of the video with the 3D geometry of the hands.

### 3.3 Action Representation and Query Prediction
Hands are represented using the parametric MANO 3D hand model, capturing joint rotations, wrist positions in camera space, and hand existence probabilities. Interestingly, while the video is generated iteratively from noise via a diffusion process (Flow Matching), the action sequence is predicted directly across all frames in a single forward pass. When actions are unobserved (during Perceive or Plan), instead of adding noise, learnable query tokens are provided as inputs for prediction.

### 3.4 Optimization and 3.5 Inference (Leveraging Goal Images)
During training, a Flow Matching loss is applied to unobserved video latents, while MANO parameters, 3D joint positions, and velocity/acceleration smoothness losses are applied to actions.
During inference, especially for tasks requiring long horizons, text instructions alone leave spatial ambiguities, such as how far apart to place objects. P³-WAM can accept a goal image (visual subgoal) as an explicit spatial target, preventing cumulative placement drift along the way (Figure F4).

captions.F3: Network architecture of P³-WAM. While sharing base weights of the video DiT, an Action Expert equipped with LoRA is deployed on the action side. Video tokens and action query tokens are concatenated and interact bidirectionally through shared attention.
captions.F4: The effect of visual goal images. (a) A goal image explicitly defines spacing between blocks that remains ambiguous with text instructions alone. (b) In long-horizon tasks, providing intermediate subgoal images prevents the accumulation of placement errors and maintains accurate assembly.

sections.heading: Synergies from unified training and real-robot verification
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted across four real-world and benchmark datasets (EgoDex, ARCTIC, HOT3D, and EgoLive). Unified training improved performance across all modes, surpassing specialized baselines, and successful action transfer to a real robot hand was demonstrated.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Does Unified Training Benefit Each Mode?
To verify whether training Perceive, Predict, and Plan together is worthwhile, the authors compared single-mode models against the unified model, all starting from the same base model.
- Perceive: Unified training reduced wrist-aligned local pose error (RR-MPJPE) by 14.23% and global camera-space error by 23.46%.
- Predict: PSNR improved from 17.356 dB to 18.138 dB, and FVD (measuring feature similarity in video) improved significantly from 1105.95 to 1009.84.
- Plan: In VLM-based video evaluation, scores jumped across all five categories, including temporal consistency (2.15 to 3.57) and goal transition (1.98 to 3.29). This provides clear evidence that the three capabilities mutually reinforce each other.

### 4.2 Perceive Evaluation: 3D Hand Reconstruction
The model was compared against state-of-the-art 3D hand reconstruction methods like HaMeR and Dyn-HaMR (Figure F5). On an evaluation metric accounting for hand existence (MPJPE-p), the proposed method achieved a camera-space error of 63.05 mm, vastly outperforming HaMeR (145.34 mm) and Dyn-HaMR (231.54 mm). By combining the temporal context of the full video with the generative model's motion prior, it reconstructs smooth 3D hands without confusing left and right hands or losing track of them during occlusions.

### 4.3 Predict Evaluation: Video World Prediction
Comparisons were made against Wan2.2-Fun-Control, EgoSim, DreamDojo, and others (Figure F6). The proposed method achieved the highest PSNR (19.020 dB) and lowest FVD (621.73) averaged across four datasets. Because explicit hand and camera control is effective, it renders physical manipulation outcomes faithfully without objects distorting or vanishing mid-video as seen in other baselines.

### 4.4 Plan Evaluation and Application to Real Robots
When videos generated in Plan mode were scored by a VLM, they received significantly higher ratings than video generation baselines like Cosmos and Wan2.2 (Figure F7). The generated human hand trajectories were also successfully converted into joint commands for a multi-fingered dexterous robot hand using the "Do as I Do" method and executed directly in a physical environment (Figure F8).

captions.F5: Qualitative comparison in Perceive mode. In baselines indicated by red boxes (HaMeR and Dyn-HaMR), hands are lost (false negatives), left and right are confused, or poses fail. In contrast, the proposed method (Ours) leverages full video context to reconstruct accurate, robust 3D hands.
captions.F6: Qualitative comparison in Predict mode. In scenes manipulating scissors or cups, objects melt or deform in conventional world models. P³-WAM predicts the future while preserving hand contact and object identities.
captions.F7: Comparison of generated results in Plan mode. In a plate-placing task, baselines fail to complete the placement by the time limit ($t=77$). P³-WAM progresses the action properly toward the state in the goal image and releases the plate at the target location.
captions.F8: Example deployment on a real robot. 3D human hand and camera trajectories planned from an initial image are retargeted into control commands for a real robot with multi-fingered hands, successfully executing block assembly and object relocation tasks in the real world.

sections.heading: Summary and future directions
sections.summary: P³-WAM unites perception, prediction, and planning into a single model, demonstrating the synergies of these capabilities in dexterous manipulation. It also outlines clear considerations for future work, including depth ambiguity in monocular cameras and open-loop control on real robots.
sections.details:
This paper proposed P³-WAM, a world action model that comprehensively addresses egocentric dexterous manipulation. By tightly connecting the rich visual and dynamic priors of video generation models with explicit 3D hand and camera trajectories, it realizes three tasks—Perceive, Predict, and Plan—within a single set of weights. It also presents highly insightful findings showing that training them concurrently elevates the accuracy of each specialized task.

Meanwhile, the authors candidly discuss several limitations:
- Estimating global 3D positions from monocular RGB video carries inherent distance ambiguities, making the integration of depth or tactile sensors a key next step.
- The current real-robot verification remains an open-loop (feedforward) execution that simply replays planned trajectories. Extending this to online closed-loop control to handle environmental changes and unexpected drift is necessary.

Despite these challenges, this work provides a remarkably complete roadmap for utilizing video foundation models as the "brain" (world model and policy) of robots.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation details and evaluation protocols
sections.summary: The appendix provides details on network integration hyperparameters, Action Autoencoder training specifications, and objective evaluation protocols involving VLMs and human raters.
sections.details:
The appendix covers critical experimental settings to ensure reproducibility and reliability.

### Architecture and Training Parameters
For each diffusion expert in the underlying Wan2.2 video model (for high noise and low noise), the action side incorporates LoRA with rank $r=128$ and scaling factor $\alpha=128$. The Action Codec, which compresses hands and camera poses, consists of an MLP with residual blocks. It compresses 21 joint 3D coordinates and camera poses into just three 64-dimensional tokens (left hand, right hand, camera). The Codec alone achieves extremely high precision, with joint position reconstruction errors between 0.8 and 2.6 mm.
Training was conducted on 16 NVIDIA H100 GPUs with a batch size of 16 at a resolution of $848\times 480$ (81 frames, 16 fps) for approximately 450 hours. Sampling probabilities for Perceive, Predict, and Plan were set to 0.2, 0.5, and 0.3, respectively, splitting 50/50 between fixing the mode across the entire clip and mixing modes randomly frame-by-frame.

### Objectivity of Evaluation
To avoid bias, Qwen3.8-Max was used as a blind judge to evaluate videos generated in Plan mode. The Spearman rank correlation between VLM scores and human ratings was around 0.37 to 0.60, indicating good agreement and firmly validating the soundness of the VLM evaluation.

takeaways: The powerful priors of video generation models are dramatically amplified when coupled with structured physical actions—explicit 3D hand and camera trajectories—acting as both a world model and a policy (action planner)

Rather than solving perception, prediction, and planning separately, multi-task training them in a single unified model by varying input/output masks produces positive synergies where tasks mutually enhance one another's accuracy
In precision placement tasks that remain ambiguous from text instructions alone, conditioning on visual subgoals (target images) is highly effective for suppressing cumulative error
limitations: Relying solely on monocular RGB video leaves inherent ambiguities in estimating absolute depth for hands and objects in camera space
Current real-robot evaluation relies on open-loop control that retargets and replays generated trajectories, lacking closed-loop control to correct contact deviations in real time
Large-scale training combining a video DiT with multiple 3D loss functions is computationally intensive, requiring 450 hours on 16 H100 GPUs
